title: Shared State & the Blackboard
summary: A blackboard is a shared store that multiple agents read from and write to, coordinating indirectly through data instead of direct messages. It's powerful but dangerous: concurrent writers can race and clobber each other's updates, so a usable blackboard needs namespaced keys, append-or-merge semantics, versioning, and a lock around read-modify-write — which you'll build in Python here.

subtopics.title: The blackboard model of coordination
subtopics.explanation: A blackboard is a central data store where agents post partial results and read what others have posted, coordinating through the shared data rather than by messaging each other directly. Each agent watches for the inputs it needs and contributes its piece, like specialists writing on a shared whiteboard. This indirect, data-centric coordination is what distinguishes the blackboard from the message-passing patterns in earlier topics.

subtopics.title: Agents read inputs and write outputs
subtopics.explanation: Instead of being handed arguments, a blackboard agent pulls the keys it depends on and posts its result under its own key, so the store becomes the single source of truth for progress. This decouples agents: a writer doesn't need to know who produced the facts, only that they exist under a known key. Reading dependencies and writing results through one store is the mechanism that lets agents work without wiring them directly together.
subtopics.example:
def researcher(bb):
    bb.write("facts", ["Paris: capital of France"])

def writer(bb):
    facts = bb.read("facts")          # pull dependency
    if facts is None:
        return                        # not ready yet
    bb.write("summary", f"Summary: {facts[0]}")

bb = Blackboard()
researcher(bb)
writer(bb)
print(bb.read("summary"))   # Summary: Paris: capital of France

subtopics.title: Races and clobbering are the core danger
subtopics.explanation: When two agents read the same key, modify it, and write back, the slower writer overwrites the faster one's change — a lost update, or 'clobbering'. This is a classic read-modify-write race and it silently drops work with no error. Recognising that naive shared writes lose data under concurrency is the whole reason a blackboard needs disciplined access, not just a dict.
subtopics.example:
# BUG: two agents append to the same list unsafely
def add_finding(bb, finding):
    items = bb.read("findings") or []   # read
    items.append(finding)               # modify (on a stale copy!)
    bb.write("findings", items)         # write -> can clobber a concurrent add

# if agent A and agent B both read [] then write, one finding is LOST
# the last writer wins and the other's append vanishes

subtopics.title: Namespacing and append semantics reduce collisions
subtopics.explanation: Give each agent its own key or namespace so independent writers never touch the same slot, and prefer append/merge operations over whole-value overwrites for shared collections. If agents write to bb['findings'][agent_id] instead of a single bb['findings'], concurrent writes don't collide at all. Designing the key layout and using additive operations is the cheapest way to avoid most clobbering before you even reach for locks.
subtopics.example:
# namespaced: each agent owns its own slot -> no collision
def post_finding(bb, agent_id, finding):
    bucket = bb.read("findings") or {}
    bucket[agent_id] = finding        # different keys, no clobber
    bb.write("findings", bucket)

# or an atomic append operation on the store itself
bb.append("log", f"{agent_id} done")   # store handles the merge safely

subtopics.title: Lock the read-modify-write when sharing a slot
subtopics.explanation: When agents genuinely must update the same value, wrap read-modify-write in a lock (or use an atomic store operation) so only one agent mutates the slot at a time and no update is lost. A version number lets a writer detect that the value changed under it and retry. Serialising the critical section is the definitive fix for clobbering, and it's exactly what you'll implement in the lab below.

foundations.overview: The blackboard pattern coordinates agents through shared data rather than direct messages: a central store holds partial results, each agent reads the keys it depends on and writes its own contribution, and the store becomes the single source of truth for progress. It decouples agents nicely — a consumer doesn't care who produced a key, only that it exists — but it introduces the classic hazard of shared mutable state. When two agents perform a read-modify-write on the same key concurrently, the last writer overwrites the other's change, silently losing an update ('clobbering'). A production-worthy blackboard therefore combines several defenses: namespacing so independent writers own separate slots, append/merge semantics instead of whole-value overwrites for shared collections, versioning so a writer can detect a value changed under it, and a lock (or atomic store operation) around any read-modify-write that must share a slot. In this hands-on topic you build a small blackboard in Python and make it safe under concurrent writers.
foundations.formalDefinition: A blackboard is a shared, centralized data store through which multiple agents coordinate indirectly by reading dependencies and writing results under keys. Correct concurrent use requires serializing read-modify-write on shared keys (via locking, atomic operations, or optimistic versioning) to prevent lost updates, and is aided by key namespacing and additive (append/merge) write semantics.
foundations.whyItMatters: Many multi-agent systems — especially those with parallel workers — need a place to accumulate shared results. Doing this with a naive dict works in demos and loses data the moment two agents write concurrently; understanding races and the standard fixes is what makes shared-state coordination safe in production.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a physical whiteboard in a war room. Analysts post findings and read each other's notes without talking directly — that's the coordination win. But if two people erase and rewrite the same corner at once, one person's note is lost. A lock is the rule 'only one marker on that corner at a time'; namespacing is 'everyone gets their own section'.
foundations.whenToUse: Use a blackboard when several agents (often parallel) must accumulate or share evolving state and you want them decoupled from each other. Prefer direct handoffs or a supervisor when coordination is simple, sequential, or when a single owner of the plan is clearer than a free-for-all on shared data.
foundations.tradeoffs: You gain decoupling and a single source of truth for progress; you take on all the hazards of shared mutable state — races, lost updates, stale reads, and lock contention. The mitigations (namespacing, append semantics, versioning, locking) add complexity and, if overused, serialize otherwise-parallel work.
foundations.performanceImpact: A coarse lock around every write serializes agents and can erase the benefit of running them in parallel; namespacing per-agent keys and locking only the truly shared read-modify-write critical section keeps most work concurrent while still preventing clobbering.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Parallel research workers posting findings to a shared board a synthesizer reads, coding agents recording per-file diffs and a shared build status, and planning systems where multiple experts contribute hypotheses to a common store that a controller evaluates.
commonUseCases: Parallel workers accumulating findings for a synthesizer
Shared progress/status store across specialist agents
A common hypothesis space multiple experts contribute to
Decoupling producers and consumers via known keys

commonMisconceptions.myth: A shared dict is a fine blackboard.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It works until two agents write concurrently; read-modify-write on the same key silently loses an update. You need namespacing, append semantics, or a lock.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Locking everything makes the blackboard correct and is basically free.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Correct, but a coarse lock serializes agents and can wipe out parallelism; lock only the shared critical section and namespace independent writes.
They're a different coordination style (indirect, via data). Simple or sequential coordination is often clearer with a supervisor or explicit handoffs.

interactiveExamples.title: A naive blackboard and the lost-update race
interactiveExamples.explanation: A plain-dict blackboard where two agents each read the shared 'findings' list, append, and write back. Simulating an interleaving where both read the same stale value shows one append silently disappearing.

code.caption: Both agents read the same empty snapshot, so B's write overwrites A's — 'A: found X' vanishes. This is a lost update.

interactiveExamples.title: A locked, atomic-append blackboard is race-free
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same scenario with an atomic append guarded by a lock. Even with real threads hammering the board concurrently, every append is preserved because the read-modify-write runs inside the critical section.

code.caption: The lock makes each append atomic, so 3 workers x 50 appends yield exactly 150 items with no lost updates.

codeLab.title: Build a race-safe blackboard
codeLab.instructions: Implement a Blackboard class safe for concurrent agents. It must support: (1) write(key, value) and read(key) for whole values; (2) append(key, value) that atomically appends to a list stored at key (creating the list if absent) with NO lost updates under concurrent threads; and (3) update(key, fn) that atomically reads the current value, applies fn to it, and stores the result (read-modify-write in one critical section). Use a threading.Lock so every mutating operation is serialized. read must return a copy of lists so callers can't mutate internal state. Complete the class so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
bb = Blackboard()

# basic write/read
bb.write("x", 10)
assert bb.read("x") == 10

# read returns a copy of lists (mutating the copy must not affect the board)
bb.write("lst", [1, 2])
snap = bb.read("lst")
snap.append(999)
assert bb.read("lst") == [1, 2]

# concurrent appends: no lost updates
import threading
def worker(name):
    for i in range(100):
        bb.append("findings", f"{name}-{i}")
threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in ("A", "B", "C")]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
assert len(bb.read("findings")) == 300

# atomic update (read-modify-write) under concurrency
bb.write("counter", 0)
def bump():
    for _ in range(100):
        bb.update("counter", lambda v: (v or 0) + 1)
ts = [threading.Thread(target=bump) for _ in range(5)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
assert bb.read("counter") == 500

print("all tests passed")
hints: Guard every mutating method with `with self._lock:` so no two threads interleave a read-modify-write on the same key.
For append, do the get-or-create AND the append inside one lock block; splitting them reintroduces the race.
In read, return `list(value)` for lists so a caller mutating the returned snapshot can't corrupt the board's internal state.

checkpoints.prompt: How does a blackboard coordinate agents differently from handoffs or a supervisor?
options: Agents coordinate indirectly through shared data — reading dependencies and writing results to a central store — rather than messaging each other
It only works with exactly two agents
It removes the need for any locking
checkpoints.explanation: The blackboard is data-centric: agents post partial results and read what others posted through one store, staying decoupled. Handoffs and supervisors instead pass control or route messages explicitly between agents.

checkpoints.prompt: Why can this concurrent append lose findings?
checkpoints.code:
def add_finding(bb, finding):
    items = bb.read("findings") or []   # read
    items.append(finding)               # modify a stale copy
    bb.write("findings", items)         # write back
options: The read, modify, and write are three separate steps, so two agents can both read the same value and the second write clobbers the first — a lost update
append is not a list method
You cannot store a list on a blackboard
checkpoints.explanation: This is a read-modify-write race: with the three steps unguarded, two agents can each read the same list and write back, so the last writer overwrites the other's append. The fix is an atomic append inside a single lock (or a per-agent namespaced key).

checkpoints.prompt: With the locked SafeBoard, what does this print?
checkpoints.explanation: Because each append runs inside the lock, the read-modify-write is atomic and no update is lost: 2 threads x 10 appends give exactly 20 items every run, deterministically.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the atomic append so no concurrent update is lost.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
def append(self, key, value):
    with self._lock:
        items = self._data.get(key, [])
        items.append(value)
checkpoints.explanation: Storing the mutated list back under the key inside the same lock block completes the atomic read-modify-write, ensuring the appended value persists even if another thread was waiting to append.

theory.question: What is the blackboard pattern, and what is its central failure mode?
theory.directAnswer: A blackboard is a shared central store through which agents coordinate indirectly: each reads the keys it depends on and writes its own results, so the store is the single source of truth for progress. Its central failure mode is the read-modify-write race — when two agents read the same key, modify it, and write back concurrently, the last writer clobbers the other's change and an update is silently lost.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A data-centric coordination model where decoupled agents post and consume partial results via a common store rather than messaging each other.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets many (often parallel) agents accumulate shared state without wiring them directly together — a producer's consumers need only know the key, not who wrote it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Agents read dependency keys and write result keys; correctness under concurrency requires serializing read-modify-write on shared keys via locks, atomic store operations, or optimistic versioning, aided by namespacing and append/merge semantics.

theory.whyImportant: Parallel multi-agent systems routinely need shared accumulation; knowing that a naive dict silently loses updates — and the standard fixes — is what separates a demo from a correct system.
theory.realWorldExample: Parallel research workers append findings to a shared board a synthesizer later reads; without a lock, two simultaneous appends on the same list dropped one worker's findings until the team made append atomic.

followUps.question: How does namespacing help before you even lock?
followUps.answer: Giving each agent its own key/slot means independent writers never touch the same value, eliminating collisions without serialization.

followUps.question: What is optimistic versioning?
followUps.answer: Store a version with the value; a writer re-checks the version at write time and retries if it changed under it, avoiding lost updates without holding a lock during work.

theory.question: How do you make a blackboard safe under concurrency without destroying parallelism?
theory.directAnswer: Namespace independent writes so each agent owns its own key (no collision, no lock needed), prefer append/merge over whole-value overwrites for shared collections, and reserve locking for the genuinely shared read-modify-write critical sections only. A coarse lock around every operation is correct but serializes all agents; locking narrowly keeps most work parallel while still preventing clobbering.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A set of layered mitigations — namespacing, additive writes, versioning, and narrow locking — that trade off correctness against concurrency.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Shared mutable state is inherently race-prone, but over-locking erases the whole point of running agents in parallel, so you apply the least serialization that still guarantees no lost updates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Design keys so independent writers don't overlap; use atomic append operations where agents contribute to a common list; add a version number for the rare shared slot so writers detect and retry on conflict; and hold a lock only around the specific read-modify-write that must share a value.

theory.whyImportant: It shows judgment beyond 'add a lock' — the harder production skill is keeping the board correct while preserving the parallelism that motivated using multiple agents in the first place.
theory.realWorldExample: A team moved from one global lock to per-agent findings buckets plus an atomic merge at the end; correctness held and throughput roughly tripled because workers no longer serialized on every write.

followUps.question: When is a single global lock actually fine?
followUps.answer: When writes are infrequent or the critical sections are tiny, the contention is negligible and the simplicity is worth it — measure before optimizing.

followUps.question: How do stale reads fit in?
followUps.answer: Even without lost writes, an agent may act on a value another agent has since changed; versioning or re-reading inside the lock guards decisions that depend on the latest state.

scenario.question: Your parallel research agents write to one shared 'findings' list and occasionally results go missing under load. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The symptom is a classic lost-update race: multiple agents do read-modify-write on the same list concurrently, so the last writer clobbers the others. Confirm by reproducing with concurrent threads and checking the final count is less than the total appends. Fix by making the append atomic — guard the read-modify-write with a lock or use an atomic append operation — and, to preserve parallelism, namespace findings per agent (a dict keyed by agent id) and merge at the end instead of contending on one list.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A concurrency bug in shared-state coordination where unsynchronized writes to a common collection drop data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reading the list, appending, and writing back are separate steps; without serialization two agents read the same version and one write overwrites the other.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Reproduce with N threads each appending K items and assert the result has N*K entries; it won't. Then wrap the append in a lock so the critical section is atomic, or switch to per-agent keys so writers never share a slot, merging results once at fan-in.

scenario.whyImportant: It exercises the exact hazard of blackboards and the two canonical fixes (serialize the critical section vs eliminate sharing via namespacing), plus the trade-off of locking against parallelism.
scenario.realWorldExample: Under load a research agent's findings count came up short intermittently; a threaded repro showed 300 appends yielding ~270 items, and switching to a locked atomic append restored all 300 while per-agent buckets kept the workers running in parallel.

followUps.question: Why does the bug only show under load?
followUps.answer: The race needs two agents to interleave their read-modify-write; low concurrency rarely overlaps, so the lost update appears only when writes collide under load.

followUps.question: How would you prevent regressions?
followUps.answer: Add a concurrency test that spawns many threads appending a known total and asserts the exact final count, so any reintroduced race fails CI.

coding.question: Implement a thread-safe blackboard with an atomic append(key, value) that never loses updates under concurrent writers.
coding.thoughtProcess: The danger is a read-modify-write race on a shared list. To guarantee no lost updates, the get-or-create of the list and the append must happen inside one critical section, so I hold a threading.Lock across the whole operation. I also return copies of lists from read so callers can't mutate internal state outside the lock. A generic update(key, fn) generalizes atomic read-modify-write for non-list values.
lineByLine: A single threading.Lock guards every mutating method so no two threads interleave a read-modify-write.
read returns list(v) for lists, handing back a snapshot copy so a caller mutating it can't corrupt the board.
append does the get-or-create AND the append inside one lock block — splitting them would reintroduce the race.
update generalizes atomic read-modify-write: it applies fn to the current value and stores the result under the lock.
The __main__ block launches 3 threads x 100 appends and prints 300, proving no updates were lost.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per append/write/update (lock acquire plus a dict op and list append); read is O(k) to copy a length-k list.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the stored data, plus O(k) per read to return a copy of a length-k list.

followUps.question: How would you avoid serializing all agents on one lock?
followUps.answer: Namespace writes per agent (a dict keyed by agent id) so independent writers never share a slot, or shard locks per key, reserving one lock per truly shared value.

followUps.question: How could you do this without a lock?
followUps.answer: Use optimistic versioning: store a version with the value, and in update re-read and compare the version at write time, retrying on mismatch (compare-and-swap) instead of holding a lock.

keyTakeaways: A blackboard coordinates agents indirectly through a shared store — they read dependencies and write results instead of messaging each other.
The core hazard is the read-modify-write race: concurrent writers clobber each other and silently lose updates.
Namespace independent writes (per-agent keys) and prefer append/merge over whole-value overwrites to avoid most collisions.
Guard any truly shared read-modify-write with a lock (or an atomic store op) so the critical section is serialized and no update is lost.
Lock narrowly, not globally: over-locking serializes agents and erases the parallelism that motivated the blackboard.
